bigPicture.subtitle: Grace That Trains a People for Good Works
paragraphs: Picture a rugged island in the Mediterranean Sea: Crete, with its mountains, harbours and many small cities. Cretans had been in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, hearing the apostles speak “the mighty works of God” (Acts 2:11), and churches had since sprung up across the island. But they were young, unorganised and vulnerable. False teachers were upsetting whole households for money. Even the island's own poet said its people had a reputation as liars and lazy gluttons. Into this setting Paul sent Titus, and then wrote him this short, powerful letter.

Titus was one of Paul's most trusted co-workers. He was a Greek, uncircumcised, whom Paul took to Jerusalem as living proof that Gentiles are saved by grace without the law: “But not even Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised” (Galatians 2:3). Later Paul sent him to sort out the troubled Corinthian church and to organise its giving. Paul calls him “my partner and fellow worker for you” (2 Corinthians 8:23). He was the man for hard assignments.

The letter was probably written between 1 Timothy and 2 Timothy, after Paul's release from his first Roman imprisonment, while he was travelling again. It shares many themes with 1 Timothy: appointing godly elders, silencing false teachers and teaching sound doctrine. But Titus is shorter and sharper. Its great theme is that truth produces godliness, and that grace produces good works. Paul uses the phrase ‘good works’ again and again, because a church in a place known for lies and laziness must show the beauty of the gospel by the way it lives.

At the heart of the letter are two of the richest summaries of the gospel in the New Testament. “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men” (Titus 2:11), training us to say no to ungodliness and to live godly lives while we wait for “the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13). And: “not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5). Titus shows that grace not only saves us but also trains us.

bridge.intro: The Holy Spirit placed Titus directly after 2 Timothy. Though Titus was most likely written earlier, it follows naturally: the dying apostle's charge to Timothy is matched by his instructions to another trusted son for building a healthy church from the ground up.

points.title: From Dalmatia Back to Crete
points.body: Near the end of 2 Timothy, Paul notes that “Titus to Dalmatia” (2 Timothy 4:10) had gone on mission to the coast of the Adriatic. The letter to Titus takes us back to an earlier assignment on Crete: “I left you in Crete for this reason, that you would set in order the things that were lacking, and appoint elders in every city, as I directed you” (Titus 1:5). The same faithful worker who stayed at his post on Crete was still serving at the end of Paul's life.

points.title: From ‘They Will Not Listen to Sound Doctrine’ to ‘Say What Fits Sound Doctrine’
points.body: 2 Timothy warned, “For the time will come when they will not listen to the sound doctrine” (2 Timothy 4:3). Titus gives the positive programme: “But say the things which fit sound doctrine” (Titus 2:1). ‘Sound’ (ὑγιαίνω) means healthy. Titus is to teach healthy doctrine and to show what a healthy church looks like — old and young, men and women, slaves and free, all living lives that fit the truth.

points.title: From ‘Equipped for Every Good Work’ to ‘Zealous for Good Works’
points.body: 2 Timothy said that God-breathed Scripture makes the man of God “thoroughly equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:17). Titus shows what that equipment is for. Christ died to make for Himself “a people for his own possession, zealous for good works” (Titus 2:14). Believers must be “ready for every good work” (Titus 3:1) and “careful to maintain good works” (Titus 3:8). No New Testament letter mentions good works more often for its size.

points.title: From ‘Loved His Appearing’ to ‘The Grace of God Has Appeared’
points.body: 2 Timothy promised a crown “to all those who have loved his appearing” (2 Timothy 4:8). Titus explains both appearings. The first: “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men” (Titus 2:11). The second: we are “looking for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13). Christian life is lived between the two, trained by the first and longing for the second.

coreTheme.title: Grace That Saves, Grace That Trains
paragraphs: The letter's core is that the grace of God both saves and trains. “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men, instructing us to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we would live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age” (2:11–12). The word for ‘instructing’ (παιδεύω) means to train a child. Grace is not only a pardon; it is a teacher. It tells us what to say no to and what to say yes to.

Salvation itself is entirely God's work: “not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit” (3:5). We contribute nothing to it. God's “kindness” and His “love toward mankind” appeared in Christ (3:4); He poured out His Spirit richly (3:6); He justified us by grace and made us heirs of eternal life (3:7).

But the salvation that is not by works is always for good works. Christ “gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works” (2:14). Immediately after the great summary of grace in chapter 3, Paul writes: “so that those who have believed God may be careful to maintain good works” (3:8). Good works are not the root of salvation, but they are its fruit.

That is why truth and life cannot be separated in this letter. It opens with “the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness” (1:1). The false teachers “profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (1:16). In contrast, the church must live in a way that will “adorn the doctrine of God, our Savior, in all things” (2:10). The beauty of the gospel is to be seen in the lives of ordinary believers.

truths.intro: As we journey through these 3 chapters, the Holy Spirit wants to anchor these truths in your spirit:

items.title: Healthy Doctrine Produces Healthy Lives
items.body: Paul keeps using the word ‘sound’, which means healthy. Sound doctrine is not dry theory; it is what makes people spiritually healthy. Elders must hold to “the faithful word which is according to the teaching, that he may be able to exhort in the sound doctrine” (1:9). When the truth is taught and believed, it shapes character: sober-minded, self-controlled, loving, reverent and kind.

items.title: Grace Is Your Teacher
items.body: The grace that saves you also trains you. It teaches you to deny ungodliness and worldly desires and to live sensibly, righteously and godly now, while you wait for Christ's appearing (2:11–13). You are not left to change yourself by willpower. God's grace, given through Christ and applied by His Spirit, is patiently training you.

items.title: Saved by Mercy, Ready for Good Works
items.body: You were saved “not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy” (3:5). That frees you from trying to earn God's love. And it frees you to do good, not to be saved, but because you are saved. Believers are to be “ready for every good work” (3:1) — practical, useful, generous, and a blessing to the people around them.

preparation.intro: Before we step into Chapter 1, prepare your spirit with these reflections:

items.title: Does Your Life Adorn the Gospel?
items.body: Paul wants believers' lives to ‘adorn’ the teaching about God, as jewels adorn a crown. Think about your daily conduct at home, at work and in your community. Would those who watch you find the gospel more beautiful, or less? Ask God to show you one area where your life does not yet fit what you believe.

items.title: Where Has Grace Been Training You?
items.body: Grace is a teacher. Think back over the last year. Where has God been saying ‘no’ to something in your life, and ‘yes’ to something else? Thank Him for His patient training, and ask Him to make you teachable as you study this letter.

prayerOfActivation: “Father, I come to Your letter to Titus, written to strengthen young churches on an island known for lies and laziness. Thank You that Your grace has appeared, bringing salvation to all people. Thank You that You saved me not because of works I had done, but because of Your mercy, through the washing of new birth and the renewing of the Holy Spirit, whom You poured out on me richly through Jesus Christ my Saviour. Let Your grace train me to say no to ungodliness and worldly desires, and to live sensibly, righteously and godly in this present age. Give me a love for sound, healthy teaching. Make me sober-minded, self-controlled, a lover of good and ready for every good work. Let my life adorn the teaching about You in all things. Raise up godly leaders in Your church, and protect Your people from those who profess to know You but deny You by their deeds. And keep my eyes fixed on the blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!”
